name: Diego Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Would you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Diego Hansen, 43, and I work as a junior construction hand doing carpentry and general site tasks. My partner and two school-age children live with me; I get a lot of satisfaction from seeing a frame stand straight, even when I come home sore.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What takes up most of your day on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I unload timber, mark pieces, help fit frames and carry waste to the skip. I use an AI chat tool most days to explain a tool I have not used before, but the supervisor still checks my measurements because I am learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a faster order list is handy if the right sheets arrive on time. I would still want someone on site to compare it with the actual room before we cut anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect a small office shortcut to replace lifting or fitting on my crew. The tight part is money; less than a month of savings does not cover a quiet spell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the shifts the supervisor offers and ask before Friday what is coming next week. When my pay is short, I would hold off on a household purchase rather than use credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small change does not sound like a reason to leave the trade. I still feel uneasy about the pay gap if a builder has no site ready for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What routine task might get a little faster in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may spend less time checking quantities before ordering. I would look over the load against the room measurements because one wrong batch can leave us waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a shorter week affect your family this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay a purchase that is not urgent and keep the children’s regular needs covered first. My partner and I would look at the next bill dates before agreeing to anything extra.

say: **I would say** a faster order list helps if the right sheets arrive on time.
**I would still want** someone to compare it with the room before we cut.
think: I do not expect a **small office shortcut** to replace lifting or fitting on my crew.
I have **thin savings**, so a quiet spell would be hard to cover.
do: Take **offered shifts** and ask the supervisor before Friday what is planned next week.
**Hold off** on a household purchase rather than use credit after a short-pay week.
feel: **Small changes** do not make me leave, but gaps between site jobs still unsettle me.
S0.quote: I would look over the load against the room measurements because one wrong batch can leave us waiting.
fieldNote: **Physical tasks** seem little changed in this mild scenario.
**Thin savings**, rather than AI, make a slow month difficult for his household.
He checks the **delivered material** against the room measurements.

steps.text: Take offered site shifts and ask before Friday about next week
Delay non-urgent household purchases after a short-pay week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say there is no shame in using a tool to get a clean list or schedule. I would also say we have to check the list against the building, because the screen cannot see a crooked opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI to explain new tools and help me study basic measurements. If the office takes over more planning, I could lose some of the simple tasks I help with, but that alone does not tell me how many site jobs builders will offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the site tablet access and practise checking its material plan against one real room. I would keep my current shifts and use the AI chat tool to learn names for tools I have not handled yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more curious than frozen because I already try these tools at home. The pay risk still bothers me, since learning does not guarantee a builder will have work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before trusting an AI material plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the screen against the drawing and the actual opening before the cutting starts. If they do not match, I would stop and ask the supervisor before we waste a full sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How could your current AI use help you learn without hiding what you still need to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can ask it to explain why a measurement matters, then test that on the job with someone experienced watching. I would not let an answer on my phone stand in for the supervisor checking my work.

say: **I would say** there is no shame in using a tool for a clean list or schedule.
**I would still check** the list against the building because the screen cannot see a crooked opening.
think: I **already use AI** to learn tools and basic measurements.
I could lose **simple tasks**, but that alone does not show how many site jobs builders will offer.
do: Practise checking the **AI material plan** against one actual room on the site tablet.
Keep taking my **current shifts** and use AI to study unfamiliar tools.
feel: **I feel curious** because I already try these tools, though learning does not guarantee site work.
S1.quote: I would not let an answer on my phone stand in for the supervisor checking my work.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** makes him willing to practise with a site tool.
He still values **human checking** and does not treat preparation as a job guarantee.

steps.text: Practise checking an AI material plan against a room on the site tablet
Keep taking current carpentry shifts while learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a robot has not arrived on site yet, but full thinking AI changes the office work first. I would not tell the crew that our physical tasks are guaranteed to remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do my basic measurement notes and the planning questions I help answer, so those parts of my job may be gone in 2028. I could still be needed for carrying and fitting until 2031, but no one has promised me paid work through that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask a skilled worker to watch me fit a door frame and correct my measuring. In 2029, I would keep trying for practical shifts and put a small amount into savings only in weeks when the mortgage and food are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives me little time to become reliable at more parts of the trade. I would still practise now, but I cannot make a confident promise about my pay after the office work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours fell after thinking AI arrived, what would you change first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop anything optional and protect the children’s school costs and the mortgage first. I would tell the children why a family plan had to wait instead of pretending we could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the later robot date change in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives some time to build practical skill if the sites keep operating and hiring. I would ask two builders nearby about work if my shifts stopped, but I would not count on finding a vacancy.

say: **I would say** full thinking AI changes office work first, before robots reach the site.
**I would not tell** the crew that our physical tasks are guaranteed to remain.
think: I think AI could do my **measurement notes** and planning questions by 2028.
I may still be needed for carrying and fitting until 2031, but no **paid work** is promised.
do: Practise fitting **door frames** with an experienced worker before 2028.
**In 2029**, I would keep seeking practical shifts and save a little only after essentials are covered.
feel: **Two years** gives me little time to become reliable at more parts of the trade.
I cannot promise what **my pay** will be once office tasks change.
S2.quote: I could still be needed for carrying and fitting until 2031, but no one has promised me paid work through that gap.
fieldNote: **Thinking tasks** may disappear before robots arrive.
**The 2029 plan** protects essentials first and does not assume a nearby vacancy.
**Thin savings** limit how long he can wait for work without pay.

steps.text: Practise fitting door frames with an experienced worker before 2028
In 2029, save a little after essential household bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time to practise more of the work while an experienced person can still correct me. I would not say that practice guarantees a job when the tools change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AI could handle the planning and measurement notes that I use to support the crew. Robots arriving around 2034 could affect the carrying and fitting too, so I cannot treat the early years as a safe career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the next few years to practise frames, trim and basic repairs with someone checking my work. In 2032, I would ask what local builders are hiring for before paying for any course or changing fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes the learning plan feel possible because I can start with one task at a time. It still worries me that a better skill may not turn into a full week of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task would you try to learn next, and how would you practise it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to fit window trim with the supervisor checking the corners and cuts. I could then use an AI tool to quiz me on the measurements at home, but I would judge my skill by the real fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to hear before spending on a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a builder to name the jobs that certificate is needed for and whether they expect to hire. If that is unclear, I would keep practising at work and not borrow for a guess.

say: **I would say** five years lets me practise more work while an experienced person can correct me.
**I would not claim** practice guarantees a job after the tools change.
think: By 2031, AI could handle the **planning notes** I use to support the crew.
I expect **robots around 2034** to affect carrying and fitting, so I cannot treat early work as a protected career.
do: **Practise frames and trim** with someone checking my work before 2031.
**In 2032**, I would ask local builders what they hire for before paying for a course or changing fields.
feel: **One task** at a time makes the five-year learning plan feel possible.
I worry better skills may not turn into a **full week of wages**.
S3.quote: I could then use an AI tool to quiz me on the measurements at home, but I would judge my skill by the real fitting.
fieldNote: He combines **AI practice** with hands-on work, judging skill by the real fitting.
Training stays conditional on **named jobs** and actual hiring needs nearby.
**Unpaid training** would require borrowing while the mortgage is tight.

steps.text: Practise fitting frames, trim and basic repairs with supervision
In 2032, check hiring needs before paying for training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years lets a family watch what is changing and make a few choices along the way. I would also say no one should mistake a long warning for a promise that their job stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes and planning I sometimes help with may be done by AI in 2036, and robots may reach site work in 2039. My children will be older by then, so their school and household costs may not look like they do today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning a practical task each year when a site can give me paid practice. In 2037, my partner and I would talk with our older child about study options when subject choices are near, rather than guess now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to use the AI tools I already know and improve my hands-on work. The mortgage is still due every month, and I cannot tell whether the later robot date leaves me a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what your children study now because of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not push them toward a trade just because I work on sites. When the older child chooses subjects, we can see what they like and what paths are actually available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could practise for several years and notice whether nearby builders still need junior workers. I would have to balance that with the mortgage and whatever the children need as they get older.

say: **I would say** ten years lets families watch and make choices along the way.
**I would warn** that a long lead time does not promise a job stays.
think: I expect AI to take some **planning notes** by 2036, with robots reaching sites in 2039.
**My children** will be older, and household needs may change by then.
do: Keep learning a practical task each year when **paid practice** is available.
**In 2037**, I would talk with my partner and older child about study options near subject choices.
feel: **More time to improve** helps, but the mortgage remains due and later work is uncertain.
S4.quote: I would have to balance that with the mortgage and whatever the children need as they get older.
fieldNote: He values the **long warning** as time to prepare, not a promise of a safe trade.
His **family plans** may change as the children get older and costs shift.

steps.text: Learn another practical construction task each year when paid practice is available
In 2037, discuss the older child’s study options with partner and child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives the shortest time to build skills or savings. I would value paid practice on real jobs and enough steady shifts to keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I learn quickly when someone lets me try the tool on the actual job and checks what I did. Junior workers still need patient teaching, even when AI can explain a measurement on a phone.

headlineQuote: Junior workers still need patient teaching, even when AI can explain a measurement on a phone.
portrait: Diego is a **43-year-old junior construction worker** supporting his partner and two school-age children.
His **thin savings** leave little room for a short spell without site wages.
He uses **AI tools daily** and learns quickly when he can test them on the job.
He is willing to **practise new tasks**, but does not assume future work is guaranteed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him little time to build skills or savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** on real jobs and steady shifts would help him keep the mortgage current.
